\chapter{River and Road}
\label{ch:ka-river-road}
\hlchaptermodality{55}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the water, the ground and the road around a Kannada village, and ask my way with them.}

Complete KA-C55-path and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[nadi]{\kn{ನದಿ} (nadi) — a river}

\label{lesson:KA-C55-river}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run: what did \emph{bēru} mean, and what did \emph{bīja} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ನದಿ}}
\textbf{\kn{ನದಿ}} (\emph{nadi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a river\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{nadī}, and under it a root \emph{nad-} meaning \textquotedblleft{}to roar, to sound\textquotedblright{}. A river is named for the noise it makes. That is a word coined by somebody who heard one before they ever saw one, in the dark, in the rain.

Kannada's own river-word is \kn{ಹೊಳೆ} (\emph{hoḷe}), and it opens with the \emph{h} you have learned to read as an old \emph{p}. \kn{ಹೊಳೆ} is the water you can walk to — the stream behind the village. \kn{ನದಿ} is the \kn{ಕಾವೇರಿ}. The borrowed word took the big rivers and left the small ones to the inherited one, which is the opposite of what usually happens.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things you would have to name to ask your way.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nadi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{nadi elli?} — \textquotedblleft{}where is the river?\textquotedblright{} — with the asking word at the end
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ನದಿ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a river\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kere]{\kn{ಕೆರೆ} (kere) — a tank, a reservoir}

\label{lesson:KA-C55-tank}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nadi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಕೆರೆ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಕೆರೆ}} (\emph{kere}) — \textquotedblleft{}a tank, a reservoir\textquotedblright{}.

English has no comfortable word for this, which is why the Indian English one is \emph{tank}. A \kn{ಕೆರೆ} is not a lake. It is built: an earth bund thrown across a shallow valley so the \kn{ಮಳೆಗಾಲ} water stands instead of running away, and so a \kn{ರೈತ} downstream still has \kn{ನೀರು} in the dry months.

The Deccan is dry and the rain arrives all at once, so this is the thing the land needed most, and Karnataka has thousands of them, many of them eight or nine hundred years old and still in use. Bengaluru's own neighbourhoods are named after the ones it has built over.

\kn{ಕೆರೆ} is inherited, and it is one of those words that tells you what its speakers were doing.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: water that runs, and water somebody stopped.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kere}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{nadi}, then \emph{kere}, and say which one of them people made
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಕೆರೆ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a tank, a reservoir\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[beṭṭa]{\kn{ಬೆಟ್ಟ} (beṭṭa) — a hill}

\label{lesson:KA-C55-hill}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kere} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಬೆಟ್ಟ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಬೆಟ್ಟ}} (\emph{beṭṭa}) — \textquotedblleft{}a hill\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, and it opens with the \emph{b} the previous chapter set beside everybody else's \emph{v}, so you can hear which layer of the language it belongs to before you know anything else about it.

Kannada distinguishes sizes here where English shrugs. \kn{ಗುಡ್ಡ} (\emph{guḍḍa}) is the small rise you would walk up without planning to; \kn{ಬೆಟ್ಟ} is the one that has a temple on top and a name on the map. \kn{ನಂದಿ} \kn{ಬೆಟ್ಟ} north of Bengaluru and \kn{ಚಾಮುಂಡಿ} \kn{ಬೆಟ್ಟ} above Mysuru are both \kn{ಬೆಟ್ಟ}, and nobody would call either a \kn{ಗುಡ್ಡ}.

A hill with a name is a hill people climb for a reason, and in Karnataka the reason is usually at the summit.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and the first of them that stands up.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{beṭṭa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{doḍḍa beṭṭa}, then \emph{cikka guḍḍa}, and hear the size words doing the sorting
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಬೆಟ್ಟ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a hill\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[haḷḷi]{\kn{ಹಳ್ಳಿ} (haḷḷi) — a village}

\label{lesson:KA-C55-village}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{beṭṭa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಹಳ್ಳಿ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಹಳ್ಳಿ}} (\emph{haḷḷi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a village\textquotedblright{}.

The \emph{h} tells you what happened: an older \emph{paḷḷi} stands behind it, worn down by the same law that turned the fruit-word and the flower-word into \kn{ಹಣ್ಣು} and \kn{ಹೂವು}.

What makes this one worth stopping for is that the older shape did not disappear — it is written on road signs across the state. Hundreds of Karnataka place names end in \emph{-halli}, and hundreds more across the border end in \emph{-palli} and \emph{-pally}. Same word, one of them having passed through the Kannada law and the other not. A learner who can hear that ending can read a map as a record of a sound change.

Tamil kept \emph{paḷḷi} too and steered it a different way, toward a place of rest and then toward a school.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and this one is signposted the length of the state.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{haḷḷi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{haṇṇu}, then \emph{haḷḷi}, and hear the one law opening both
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಹಳ್ಳಿ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a village\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dāri]{\kn{ದಾರಿ} (dāri) — a way, a path}

\label{lesson:KA-C55-path}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{haḷḷi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ದಾರಿ}}
\textbf{\kn{ದಾರಿ}} (\emph{dāri}) — \textquotedblleft{}a way, a path\textquotedblright{}.

This is the word that turns the other four into directions. \kn{ಕೆರೆಗೆ} \kn{ದಾರಿ} — the way to the tank — and you already have the little \emph{-ge} that hangs on the end of the place you are heading for.

Kannada keeps a second word for the same thing, \kn{ಹಾದಿ} (\emph{hādi}), and speakers use the two close to interchangeably, though \kn{ಹಾದಿ} leans a little toward the worn track and \kn{ದಾರಿ} a little toward the route you choose.

Put \kn{ದಾರಿ} with the polite word you already have and you have the sentence a stranger needs most: \kn{ದಯವಿಟ್ಟು} \kn{ದಾರಿ} \kn{ಹೇಳಿ} — please tell me the way. Notice that nothing in it names you. Kannada lets the asking be the request.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \kn{ನದಿ}, \kn{ಕೆರೆ}, \kn{ಬೆಟ್ಟ}, \kn{ಹಳ್ಳಿ}, \kn{ದಾರಿ}. Four landmarks and the thread between them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dāri}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{dayaviṭṭu dāri hēḷi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ದಾರಿ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a way, a path\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
